items.title: P less than 0.05 doesn't mean a result is true — or even probably true
items.claim: A study finds an effect with p = 0.04. Headlines say 'statistically significant'. The reader assumes the effect is real. In fact, in some scientific fields, more than half of 'p < 0.05' findings fail to replicate.

options.text: The probability the effect is real is 96%

The probability of seeing data at least this extreme IF the null hypothesis is true is 4%. Says nothing directly about the probability the effect is real, which requires Bayesian reasoning with priors
The result is wrong 4% of the time
P-values measure the size of effects

items.reveal_title: P-value misinterpretation and the replication crisis
items.reveal:
P-value definition: P(data at least as extreme as observed | null hypothesis true).

Common misinterpretations:
1. P is the probability the null is true (no).
2. (1 - p) is the probability the effect is real (no).
3. P measures effect size (no — small effects in large studies can have tiny p).
4. P < 0.05 means 'real effect' (no — depends on prior plausibility and study design).

Replication crisis (2010s): many influential findings in psychology, biomedicine, economics fail to replicate.
- Open Science Collaboration (2015) attempted to replicate 100 psychology studies. ~36% of replications succeeded (vs ~97% of original studies reporting significance).
- Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology (2021) attempted 23 cancer findings; only 25% of effects were as strong in replication.
- Many famous psychology results (ego depletion, power posing, money priming) have not replicated.

Causes:
- P-hacking (running many tests, reporting only significant ones).
- Publication bias (significant findings published; null results filed away).
- Small samples + multiple testing.
- Garden of forking paths (each analytic choice creates uncounted tests).
- Underpowered studies (true effects mixed with noise; significant results when found are overestimates).

Reforms: preregistration, registered reports, focus on effect sizes and confidence intervals, replication studies, statistical training reform, banishing the 0.05 threshold (some journals).

Bayesian alternatives: P(hypothesis | data) directly. Requires explicit priors but gives more interpretable answers.

The ASA's 2016 statement on p-values: don't use 'p < 0.05' as the sole basis for conclusions. Distance is being made from this old standard.
items.why: P-values look like simple measures of certainty. They aren't. Misinterpreting them has contributed to a massive scientific replication crisis. Understanding what p-values do and don't say is essential to reading research.

items.title: Energy can be lost in a collision; momentum cannot
items.claim: Two cars crash and lock together. Their combined kinetic energy after the collision is LESS than before (energy lost to heat, sound, deformation). But the combined momentum is exactly the same.
items.prompt: Why does momentum survive while energy doesn't?

options.text: Momentum is always conserved; energy is not

Total energy is conserved if you include heat, sound, deformation — but KINETIC energy alone is not conserved in inelastic collisions. Momentum is a vector quantity conserved by Newton's third law independent of internal energy losses
Momentum and energy are equally lost
Energy conservation only applies to electricity

items.reveal_title: Conservation laws and what they refer to
items.reveal:
Newton's third law (action and reaction) implies that internal forces in a closed system cancel pairwise. Total momentum (m1 v1 + m2 v2 + ...) does not change unless an external force acts.

This holds regardless of whether the collision is elastic (kinetic energy conserved) or inelastic (kinetic energy partly converted to heat, deformation, etc.).

Kinetic energy = (1/2) m v^2 — proportional to v squared, so velocity SIGN doesn't matter (kinetic energy is scalar and always positive). Two equal-mass objects approaching each other with v and -v have total KE > 0 but total momentum = 0. After perfectly inelastic collision (stuck together), final velocity = 0, KE = 0. KE is lost; momentum unchanged.

Elastic collisions (snooker balls, gas molecules): both momentum and kinetic energy conserved.
Inelastic collisions (cars sticking, putty hitting wall): momentum conserved; some KE -> heat/sound/deformation.
Explosions (reverse collisions): momentum still conserved (must be balanced); KE can INCREASE (from chemical energy released).

The full energy conservation includes all forms: chemical, thermal, acoustic, electromagnetic. It's the kinetic energy alone that can vary.

The distinction is crucial for understanding everything from billiard balls to particle accelerators to car crashes to firearms.
items.why: Conservation laws are taught as universal. Different conservation laws apply to different quantities and conditions. Energy is always conserved (with all forms counted); kinetic energy alone is not.

items.title: The sum of all positive integers equals minus one twelfth
items.claim: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + ... = -1/12. This obviously fails as a normal sum (it diverges to infinity). But it is the value of the Riemann zeta function analytically continued to s = -1, and it shows up in physics (Casimir effect, string theory).
items.prompt: How does an obviously divergent sum get a finite value?

options.text: Analytic continuation extends a function defined on one domain (where the series converges) to a larger domain (where the series doesn't); zeta(-1) is well-defined as a function value even though the corresponding series diverges
Negative numbers were added without permission

items.reveal_title: Ramanujan, Hardy, and the strange identity
items.reveal:
Srinivasa Ramanujan wrote to Hardy in 1913 claiming results like 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ... = -1/12. Hardy initially thought Ramanujan must be a crank — until he checked.

The Riemann zeta function is defined by zeta(s) = sum from n=1 to infinity of 1/n to the power s, but only when the real part of s exceeds 1. The function extends analytically to the whole complex plane (except a pole at s = 1). At s = -1, zeta(-1) = -1/12.

If you formally substitute s = -1 into the series, you get 1 + 2 + 3 + ... The series doesn't converge there — but the function it defined still has a value, just by a different (analytic continuation) method.

In quantum field theory, the same -1/12 appears. The Casimir force calculation involves summing zero-point energies of standing waves; this sum diverges, but the physical answer obtained by zeta regularisation matches experiment.

The identity is not casually 'true' as arithmetic. It's true as the value of a specific extension of the zeta function — and that extension happens to give physically correct predictions.
items.why: Treating divergent sums as if they have finite values seems like a trick — but in the right framework, analytic continuation gives them precise meanings that physics turns out to use.
